e.t: Abeddaram, also rendered Aveththaram, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it identifies one individual by name. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 1 Chronicles 13:14. Because the available information gives the name but not its meaning or the verse text, its precise identity and significance must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context.

This adjective means “unmarried,” describing a person who does not have a spouse. It identifies marital status rather than expressing an action or describing a particular emotion, virtue, or spiritual condition. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 16:9. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the word’s precise role in that sentence must be understood from its immediate context. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: it refers to someone who is not married.

This word is a proper name referring to a person, rendered as “Adaias” or “Atheas.” It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it identifies someone by name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 10:29. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the person’s identity and role cannot be explained beyond recognizing this word as a personal name.

Athath is a proper name, referring to a person named Athath rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:13. Because the available information gives the name but not its etymological meaning or the surrounding verse text, its significance is limited to identifying this individual. It should therefore be read as a personal name, not translated as an ordinary descriptive word.

Alema is a proper name, referring to a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Its recorded meaning is simply “Alema,” so no broader definition is supported here. In the Greek LXX corpus represented by this entry, it occurs once, at 1 Maccabees 5:35. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify exactly what Alema refers to in that passage.

Amalek is a proper name referring to a people known in the Greek Old Testament. It is not an ordinary descriptive word but the name of a distinct group. The name appears 46 times across 44 Old Testament verses in the Greek Old Testament, from Genesis through Psalms. Its repeated appearance in historical and wilderness passages shows that Amalek is a recurring people-group name within Israel’s Scriptures, while the specific significance of any occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “lie down,” describing the act of reclining or settling oneself in a lying position. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here: once in Genesis and twice in Sirach. Its basic meaning remains physical and straightforward; the surrounding verse determines whether the action is resting, reclining for a meal, or simply taking a lying position.

gl: giving one’s life in recompense for another’s
d: giving one’s life in recompense for another’s

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something giving one’s life in recompense for another’s. It expresses life offered on behalf of another person, with the idea of repayment or exchange built into the phrase. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both in 4 Maccabees. The word therefore points to a life surrendered for someone else, rather than merely mentioning life in a general sense. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse.

This adjective describes something broken sharply away or extremely steep—"broken sheer off; precipitous." It points to an abrupt, cliff-like form rather than a gradual slope. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 13:5. Because no verse text is available here, the word’s precise role in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a sharply broken or precipitous feature.

This Greek LXX verb means “destroy” or “kill”: to bring something or someone to ruin or death. As a verb, it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 6:14. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on its surrounding context, but its basic sense is the ending or removal of life or existence.

This adjective means “of silver,” describing something made from, connected with, or characterized by silver. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for silver objects and materials, including items associated with gifts, furnishings, vessels, and construction. The word occurs 81 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, with most occurrences in the Old Testament. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the noun or object it describes.

This word means “plow,” the farming implement used to break or turn soil for cultivation. It is a noun naming a physical agricultural tool. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages in 1 Chronicles, Isaiah, Joel, Micah, and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the tool itself.

This adjective describes something as unremarkable—ordinary, without special distinction or notable prominence. It can characterize a person, thing, or circumstance that does not stand out from others. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, appearing once each in Genesis, Job, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what the surrounding passage is describing.

This Greek LXX noun refers to “restriction; status.” It names either a limiting condition or a person’s or thing’s standing, depending on how it functions in its sentence. The word occurs once in the Greek Septuagint corpus, in 3 Maccabees 2:29. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the precise sense intended in that occurrence cannot be narrowed further. Its basic meaning remains centered on restriction or status rather than an action or description of emotion.

This verb means “separate”: to set something or someone apart from others. It can describe making a distinction, placing things in different groups, or designating something for a distinct purpose. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, it occurs 87 times, so it is a recurring word for division or setting apart rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on what people, objects, or groups are being distinguished.

This word means “confirmation”—something that establishes or gives assurance that a matter is firm and reliable. As a noun, it refers to the confirming act or result rather than to a person who confirms. In the Greek Old Testament and related Wisdom literature represented here, it occurs twice: once in Leviticus and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here.

Βηθελισουβ is a proper name, rendered as “Bēthelisoub” or “Vithelisuv.” It functions as the name of a person, place, or other named entity in the Greek Old Testament, rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs three times, all within two verses of Nehemiah: once in Nehemiah 3:20 and twice in Nehemiah 3:21. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be identified more precisely here.

This Greek LXX verb means “have a sore throat.” It describes a physical throat condition, expressed as an action or state rather than as a person, object, or general feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 68:4. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise role in that sentence cannot be explained beyond this basic lexical meaning. Its central sense remains a bodily condition affecting the throat.

Gadgad is a proper name, rendered “Gadgad” and also identified as “Gathgath.” It refers to a named place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times across three verses, in Numbers and Deuteronomy. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and travel-list context, but the word itself functions as a geographical name.

Gatheth is a proper name, not a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It is preserved in the Greek Old Testament and occurs once, in Joshua 21:17. The name itself is clear, but the precise person, place, or other named entity it identifies must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage. No broader lexical definition is given for Gatheth beyond its use as this proper name.

This noun refers to “juggling” or “cheatery,” naming trickery rather than honest or straightforward dealing. In ordinary terms, it describes a deceptive practice that relies on misleading skill or show. As a noun, it identifies the activity itself, not necessarily a person who performs it. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 12:24. Its central idea is the use of tricks to deceive or manipulate rather than communicate or act openly.

This word means “tree,” referring to a woody plant. It is a noun used to name such a plant rather than describe an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Deuteronomy 22:6. The word’s basic meaning is straightforward, while the precise force of the reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its single occurrence does not broaden the meaning beyond the ordinary sense of a tree.

This verb means “double”: to make something twice as much or to increase it twofold. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both in Ezekiel, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in either passage depends on what is being doubled in context.

This word means “twenty thousand.” It is an adjective used to describe a quantity, telling how many people, objects, or other things are involved. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs six times, all in 2 Maccabees. The surrounding noun and sentence determine exactly what is being counted, but the number itself remains clear: a very large amount consisting of twenty thousand units.

This adjective describes someone or something that is “hard to check” or “restless”—difficult to restrain or settle. Its central idea is a lack of calm or easy restraint, rather than a specific action by itself. Within the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:7. That reference identifies its only recorded occurrence, while the precise force of the word there depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Edna” or “Ethna.” It identifies a woman named in the Greek Old Testament tradition rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Chronicles 12:21. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide a further meaning or explanation for the name itself. Its ordinary function is simply to identify the person who bears it.

This is a verb meaning “give out.” It describes the act of giving something to another person or making it available from a source. Its central sense is an outward transfer rather than merely possessing or keeping something. In the Greek LXX, it occurs eight times, in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. The surrounding verse determines what is given and to whom.

“Voluntary” describes something done willingly, by personal choice rather than compulsion. In the Greek Old Testament, this adjective can describe an offering or gift brought freely. It therefore points to willing participation or giving, rather than an act performed only because it is required. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 13 verses, and its central idea remains consistent. Its precise force in a particular verse is clarified by the surrounding sentence.

Elie is a proper name—the personal name of an individual. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 23:37. Because a personal name identifies someone rather than describing an action or quality, its basic meaning is the person designated by that name. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain Elie’s specific role or connection in that passage.

“Eli” is a personal name, identifying someone called Eli rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Judges 5:5. The available information establishes the name and its single occurrence, but the verse text is not provided here, so no further conclusion about the person or the name’s role in that passage can be drawn from this word alone.

gl: look fixedly on; fix steadfastly on
d: look fixedly on; fix steadfastly on

e.t: This verb means “look fixedly on” or “fix steadfastly on.” It describes directing one’s gaze steadily and intently toward someone or something, rather than merely glancing at it. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 5:30. Its basic sense emphasizes a focused, persistent look; the surrounding verse is needed to determine what is being watched and why.

This Greek LXX verb means to “hurl against” or “charge upon.” It describes a forceful movement directed toward someone or something, especially an attack or assault. As a verb, it expresses the action rather than naming the attacker or the target. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX material represented here, all in the deuterocanonical books of 1 and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “sit upon”—to take a seated position on something or someone. It describes the act of settling onto a place, object, or person, rather than merely being nearby. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across eight verses, so its basic meaning remains consistent while the surrounding situation determines what is being sat upon. The word appears from Genesis through Ezekiel and is used in descriptions involving people, seats, and elevated or supporting places.

This Greek LXX verb means “run over,” describing movement in which someone or something runs across or over another place or object. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Genesis and twice in the Maccabean books. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun refers to an occupation or to effort—the work a person undertakes or the exertion given to a task. Its central idea is purposeful activity, whether viewed as someone’s regular work or as the labor required to accomplish something. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 44 times, showing that the word can describe work broadly rather than one narrow kind of task. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “wish” and can also be rendered “make.” It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 73 times, with uses spread across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is not limited to one narrow setting. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic lexical range is expressed by wishing or making.

Zaret is a proper name used as a name rather than a common description or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, with occurrences in Numbers 21:12 and Deuteronomy 2:13–14. The form is consistently identified and rendered as “Zaret,” so no broader ordinary meaning is supplied for it. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name alone does not establish further details about its referent or significance.

This Greek LXX noun means “bridle” or “rein,” the strap or control used to guide an animal. It names a physical object rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 25:9. The word’s basic sense remains simple and concrete: something placed in or attached to an animal’s mouth for directing and restraining it.

Tharsa is a proper name used to identify a specific named entity. It does not describe an action, quality, or general category; its role is simply to name someone or something called Tharsa. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Joshua 12:24. Without the surrounding verse text, the evidence supports the name itself but does not establish whether Tharsa refers to a person, place, or another named entity in that passage.

This proper name refers to Thebes, also rendered Thivis, the name of a place. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographical name used to identify a specific location. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Judges 9:50. The name itself supplies the location’s identity, while the surrounding verse and passage provide the details of what happened there.

Iaziz is a proper name, referring to a person named Iaziz rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 27:31. The available wording identifies the name itself but does not provide a broader lexical definition or meaning beyond Iaziz. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s role there.

Iezria is a proper name—the personal name of an individual in the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint). It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. This name occurs twice in the Septuagint text, both occurrences being in 1 Chronicles 7:3. The available lexical information gives the name itself, “Iezria,” but does not provide an additional ordinary-language definition or explain its etymological meaning. Its precise significance in the verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being identified there.

Ikak is a proper name referring to a person named in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is chiefly the person’s name rather than an idea to define. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 6:60. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain Ikak’s specific place in that passage; the name itself simply identifies the individual mentioned there.

Iraam is a proper name referring to a person named Iraam. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs four times, all in 1 Chronicles. Because a personal name identifies someone rather than describing an action, quality, or object, its basic meaning is the person it names: Iraam. The surrounding verse text is needed to distinguish which details about this person matter in each occurrence.

This word is a proper personal name, given as “Iōbēl; Iovil.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, all in Judges 9, between Judges 9:26 and 9:36. Since the verse text is not provided, its particular reference cannot be explained further than recognizing it as the name of a person mentioned in that passage.

This word is a proper name referring to Kadesh, also rendered Kathis. It identifies a place named in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs 38 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing from Genesis through Ezekiel. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding account, but the word itself functions as a geographical name. The supplied references include Genesis 14:7, Genesis 20:1, several passages in Numbers, and later Old Testament books.

This Greek LXX adjective means “fine; fair.” It qualifies a person, thing, or condition by describing it with that meaning, rather than naming an action or object. The word is broadly used in the Greek LXX, occurring 192 times across 186 verses, from Genesis through Song of Songs. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the noun it describes and the surrounding sentence.

Kanath is a proper name, identifying a place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 2:23. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name’s precise role in that genealogy cannot be described further. Its lexical meaning is therefore simply the name “Kanath,” preserved as a specific place-name in this Old Testament passage.

Karkar is a proper name referring to a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament. Its meaning is simply the name “Karkar”; the available lexical information does not provide an additional descriptive sense or translation. This word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Judges 8:10. Its precise referent and significance must therefore be understood from that passage’s surrounding text rather than from the name itself.

This Greek LXX verb means “leap down”: to move downward in a sudden, jumping motion. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality, so its ordinary sense is straightforward and physical. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Genesis 24:64 and 1 Samuel 25:23. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly who performs the action and why in either passage.

This noun means “boast” or “reason for boasting”—something a person takes pride in or points to with satisfaction. It can describe the object or basis of boasting, rather than the act of boasting itself. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 23 times, showing a repeated use for what is regarded as a source of honor, confidence, or proud acknowledgment. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word means “moderate,” referring to something or someone characterized by restraint rather than excess. As a noun, it can name a moderate person or quality, though its precise role depends on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ecclesiastes 12:9. The word’s basic sense is therefore a measured or restrained character, while the surrounding verse determines what is being described.

This Greek LXX noun means “sheepskin” or “fleece,” referring to the woolly covering of a sheep or the hide associated with it. It names a physical material rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Nehemiah 3:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a sheep’s fleece or skin.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “hew in stone”: to cut or shape stone by striking or carving it. It describes deliberate work done to produce a prepared stone surface or object, rather than merely moving or breaking stone. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages concerning stone tablets and carved places. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and object being shaped.

This word means “linen,” describing something made from the flax-based material used for cloth and garments. In the Greek Old Testament, it is an adjective, so it identifies clothing or other objects by their material rather than naming a person, action, or spiritual quality. It occurs 15 times across 10 verses, especially in Leviticus, and is used in passages concerning garments and fabric. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense remains material: linen.

Maisa, also rendered Mesa, is a proper name used to identify a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 8:36–37. Since the word is a personal name rather than a descriptive term, its meaning is primarily its identifying role: it distinguishes one individual within the genealogical record. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain that person’s specific place or significance in the passage.

Menestheus is a proper name identifying a person. Its meaning is therefore primarily a personal designation rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 2 Maccabees chapter 4. It is rendered “Menestheus” in the available English translation, while the lexical entry also records “Menesthefs” as a form of the name. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the person’s role in either passage.

This verb describes being anxious or taking care about something. It expresses focused concern—an inward uneasiness or active attention directed toward a person, matter, or need. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, so its basic meaning is consistent while the surrounding passage determines what the concern involves. It may describe troubling anxiety or responsible care, but the word itself centers on concern rather than indifference.

This word means “tomb,” referring to a place where the dead are laid. It is a noun used for a burial place in the Greek Old Testament. The word occurs 20 times in 19 verses across the Greek Old Testament, with uses extending from Exodus to Ezekiel. Its basic meaning remains focused on the grave or tomb itself, while the surrounding passage determines what is being said about that place in a particular verse.

This adjective describes something considered “loathsome” or “abominable”—deeply repulsive and morally detestable. It is used to characterize an object, action, or condition rather than to name a person or thing by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Leviticus 18:23. Its basic force is strong rejection: what it describes is viewed as disgusting and unacceptable. The surrounding verse is needed to identify exactly what is being described there, but the word itself communicates intense abhorrence.

Nambran, also rendered Namvran, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, though the available information does not provide enough context to determine which. This name occurs once, in Numbers 32:36, and its precise identification depends on reading that passage’s surrounding text.

Nasib, also rendered Nasiv, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a named individual in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs six times across six Old Testament verses, appearing in Joshua, 1 Samuel, and 1 Kings. Its specific reference in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named there.

This Greek LXX verb means “conquer”: to overcome an opponent or prevail against resistance. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its exact force depends on what or whom someone overcomes in the sentence. The word occurs 23 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including three Old Testament occurrences and twenty in deuterocanonical books. Its central idea remains victory over an opposing power, whether that victory is described directly or applied figuratively. The word appears from Psalms through 4 Maccabees.

Xenios, also given as Ksenios, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a particular person, place, or figure in the Greek Old Testament collection, but the available lexical information does not specify which kind of name it is. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 6:2. Its precise referent must therefore be understood from that verse and its surrounding passage.

This adjective means “all-purple,” describing something whose overall color is purple rather than something merely marked with purple. It functions as a descriptive color word, identifying the appearance of an object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Numbers 4. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the particular object being described, but the word itself emphasizes complete or uniform purple coloring.

This adjective describes people who are united in mind, sharing the same outlook or purpose. It presents agreement and inner unity rather than merely being together in the same place. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 14:20. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is clear: people are of one mind when their thinking and direction are joined.

This word means “fifteenth,” describing something that comes after the fourteenth and before the sixteenth. It is an adjective used to identify a day, date, or other numbered position. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 22 times, including passages that mark particular dates and festival times. Its meaning remains a straightforward ordinal number; the surrounding sentence identifies what is fifteenth. The word appears from Exodus through 2 Maccabees, showing repeated use for calendar and sequence references.

gl: tie the hands behind the back
d: tie the hands behind the back

e.t: This verb means “tie the hands behind the back.” It describes the physical act of binding a person’s hands so they are held behind the body, and it functions as an action word rather than a title or description of a person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:3. The word’s basic meaning is clear from its explicit definition; its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

gl: gild all over; cover with gold
d: gild all over; cover with gold

e.t: This verb means to gild something all over—to cover it with gold. It describes the action of applying a gold covering or coating, rather than merely possessing gold. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in separate verses, with two occurrences in Isaiah and one in 1 Kings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is thorough covering with gold.

This adjective describes something as “one of many”—a single member within a larger number or group. It identifies an individual instance without suggesting that it is the only one or necessarily the most important. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs twice, in 2 Samuel and Proverbs. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains a reference to one item among numerous others.

This Greek LXX verb means “overtake” or “take over.” It describes one person or thing coming ahead of another or gaining control of it. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:16. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on catching up, prevailing over something, or assuming control, but the central idea remains moving ahead of or taking hold of another.

This Greek LXX noun means “going.” It names the act or process of going rather than describing a person or object. The word occurs seven times in the LXX corpus represented here, including once in Proverbs and several times in 2 and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here.

This adjective describes something as belonging to the first beginning or as primal—present at the earliest point or standing at the origin. It can identify what is first in order or foundational in relation to what follows. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 10:11. The reference identifies its sole occurrence, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain precisely how the adjective functions there. Its central meaning remains the idea of what is first, originating, or primal.

Saaris is a proper name identifying a person or place named in the Greek Old Testament. The available lexical information gives no descriptive meaning beyond the name itself, so it should be understood as a designation rather than as a word expressing an action, quality, or teaching. In the Greek Old Testament, Saaris occurs once, in Numbers 3:27. Its precise referent and significance depend on the surrounding verse and passage, since the name alone does not explain the role of the person or place it identifies.

Sarathaioi, also rendered Sarathei, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or group in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 2:53. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the name’s specific identity cannot be explained further without adding information not provided by Scripture in this record.

Saphou, also rendered Safu, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named figure in the Greek Old Testament translation. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 20:4. Because the available information gives the name but not the verse text or a connected definition, its significance cannot be expanded beyond identifying the person named there.

“Moth-eaten” describes something damaged or consumed by moths. It is an adjective, so it identifies a condition rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Job 13:28, and its basic meaning is the literal condition of being eaten by moths. It presents the image of material weakened or spoiled by moths, while the precise force in that verse depends on its surrounding wording and passage.

This noun means “protector” or “defender”: one who shields, supports, or stands for another. It describes a person understood by the help and safety provided to others, rather than naming a place, object, or action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs five times across three Old Testament and two deuterocanonical verses. Its precise emphasis in any particular passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains someone who gives protection or defense.

This word means “equipment”: the tools, furnishings, or other items prepared for a particular use. As a noun, it refers to a collection of useful things rather than to an action or a person. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 200 times, showing that it is a normal word for material objects arranged or supplied for work, worship, travel, or other purposes. Its exact reference in any passage depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains equipment prepared for use.

This Greek LXX verb means “hurry”: to act, move, or proceed quickly. It describes prompt action rather than delay, and its exact force can depend on what someone is hurrying to do. The word occurs 62 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, showing that it is used across many kinds of narrative situations. It appears from Genesis through Susanna, including passages involving travel, urgent movement, and immediate response.

This noun means “shared training” or “training together.” It refers to people being trained alongside one another, emphasizing participation in a common exercise or discipline rather than training in isolation. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 8:18. The word itself identifies the shared nature of the training, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the specific kind of training intended there.

This verb means to yoke together—to join things or persons so they are bound or coordinated as one unit. It describes the action of placing two things under the same yoke, much as animals are joined for shared work or movement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both in Ezekiel 1, at Ezekiel 1:11 and 1:23.
